soil-env-200.title: PFAS: the 'forever chemicals' in soil and food
soil-env-200.text: A 2024 study tested 45,000 groundwater samples from areas with no obvious source of pollution and found harmful PFAS levels in 31% of them. PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are synthetic chemicals with many fluorine atoms on a carbon chain. They are so stable they are called 'forever chemicals'. Thousands have been made since Teflon in 1938, for waterproof fabrics, carpets, food packaging, firefighting foam and cosmetics. Levels peak at wastewater plants and landfills, and firefighting foam has contaminated land near airports and air bases. Soil PFAS has been found as far away as Antarctica. Contaminated soil raises PFAS in foods such as white rice, coffee and animals raised on the land. On average, concentrations double with each step up a food web, though compounds vary widely. Exposure is linked to cancers, thyroid disease, lowered immunity and fertility, and high cholesterol. Two of them, PFOS and PFOA, joined the Stockholm Convention on persistent organic pollutants in 2009 and 2019. Treatment can trap them on activated carbon or biochar, or destroy them by oxidation, plasma or incineration.

soil-env-010.title: Biomagnification: how poisons concentrate up the food chain
soil-env-010.text: Herring carry about 0.01 ppm of mercury. Sharks carry more than 1 ppm. The difference is biomagnification: the rise in a substance's concentration in the tissues of organisms at each higher level of a food chain. It differs from bioaccumulation, the build-up within one organism from its food and surroundings. Persistent, fat-soluble compounds are the classic case. DDT and other organochlorines are stable and lipophilic, or fat-loving, so they build up in bodies and food chains. Birds that ate DDT-laden prey got weaker eggshells and more chick deaths, and some species were threatened with extinction. PCBs are easily retained in organisms, so they both accumulate over a lifetime and magnify up food webs. Mercury takes a microbial detour. Bacteria and archaea turn inorganic mercury into methylmercury, which builds up in fish such as tuna and swordfish and magnifies further up the chain. Scientists measure the effect with the biomagnification factor, the ratio of predator to prey concentration. The trophic magnification factor does the same across a whole food web. Values above 1 mean magnification. Reviews suggest the effect is rarer than once thought. Still, DDT, DDE, PCBs, toxaphene, and organic mercury and arsenic clearly do biomagnify.

soil-env-045.title: Soil vapor extraction: vacuuming pollution out of the ground
soil-env-045.text: Volatile trichloroethene in permeable sand low in carbon comes out of the ground readily. Naphthalene held in clay layers takes much longer. Both fates follow from how soil vapor extraction works. It is a physical, in situ treatment that removes volatile contaminants from unsaturated soil, the {{ref:soil-water-230}}, by drawing them out as gas. Vacuum blowers and extraction wells pull gas through the ground. Contaminants move from sorbed, dissolved and pure phases into that gas, which is treated above ground. It suits contaminants with high Henry's law constants, which escape readily from water into air, such as many chlorinated solvents and hydrocarbons. The US EPA treats it as a mature presumptive remedy. It uses standard wells and off-the-shelf equipment, disturbs the site little, and treats large soil volumes at reasonable cost. But zones of low air flow, high moisture or strong adsorption cause tailing and rebound, and extraction rates typically fall over time.

soil-env-003.title: Microplastics: the plastic specks farm soils quietly collect
soil-env-003.text: Every agricultural soil sample tested in southwestern China held plastic particles, and 92% of them were microfibers. Microplastics are insoluble synthetic plastic particles between 1 micrometer and 5 millimeters across, polluting soil as well as water and air. Primary microplastics, such as clothing microfibers and pellets, are already small when released. Secondary ones form as larger plastic items weather and break apart. The Chinese fibers probably came from string, twine and irrigation water used to wash clothes. Biosolids from sewage sludge, and compost, add more. About half the sewage sludge in Europe and North America goes onto farmland. In Europe that delivers an estimated 113 to 770 tonnes of microplastics per million inhabitants to farm soils each year. Earthworms, mites and springtails may grind swallowed plastic into still smaller pieces. A 2024 meta-analysis of 180 studies found microplastics raised soil carbon dioxide emissions by 25.7% and soil organic carbon by 25.4%, and cut aboveground plant biomass. Effects depend strongly on the type of plastic. Yet most studies report only that microplastics are present, not their origin or quantity.

soil-env-038.title: Phytoextraction: harvesting pollution in leaves and stems
soil-env-038.text: Some plants mine the soil without meaning to. Phytoextraction uses plants whose roots absorb contaminants from soil or water and concentrate them in above-ground growth that can be harvested and carried away. The stars are plants that take up very high amounts, described in {{ref:soil-env-050}}. The Chinese brake fern, which accumulates arsenic, has been proposed for stripping arsenic from contaminated soil. Fast-growing ordinary plants such as poplars and willows take up little per plant. Grown in bulk, they could still remove a considerable amount. A common snag is that heavy metals are often too immobile for roots to absorb. Assisted phytoextraction adds a chelator, a compound that binds the metal and makes it more soluble. The idea even has a commercial twist. Metal-hoarding plants underpin a proposed way to collect valuable metals without excavation, described in {{ref:soil-env-051}}.

soil-env-047.title: Electrokinetic remediation: pulling metals out with electric current
soil-env-047.text: In its first test, the Lasagna Process removed 98% of the trichloroethylene from the soil. Developed at Paducah, Kentucky, in 1995, it built horizontal treatment layers through the ground. It is one form of electrokinetic remediation: passing direct current through the ground to draw organic, inorganic and heavy-metal contaminants out of soil. Anode and cathode electrodes sit in reservoir wells placed to fit the contaminant plume. An injected electrolyte conducts the current and carries contaminants away. Two motions drive it. Charged particles migrate toward the electrodes, the dominant effect, while pore fluid flows the opposite way by electro-osmosis. Contaminants must be dissolved as ions to move. Usefully, the low pH that develops keeps metals off soil particles and releases sorbed ones. Its main targets are cadmium, chromium, mercury, zinc, lead and copper. It works in situ in tight soils, removing up to 90% of heavy metals from kaolinite and clayey sands. Counterintuitively, highly permeable soils lower its efficiency. Undissolvable contaminants stay put, long runs acidify soil near the electrodes, and buried metal objects short-circuit the system.

soil-env-055.title: Biostimulation: feeding the microbes already on site
soil-env-055.text: Molasses can help clean polluted ground. Biostimulation modifies the environment to stimulate bacteria already present that can carry out bioremediation, chiefly by adding nutrients or electron acceptors or donors. Additions include phosphorus, nitrogen, oxygen and carbon sources such as molasses. For halogenated contaminants where oxygen is absent, organic electron donors let native microbes use the contaminants themselves as electron acceptors. The main advantage is the workforce. Native microbes are already suited to the subsurface and spread through it. Adding specialized cultures, described in {{ref:soil-env-032}}, can enhance the effect. Delivery is the hard part. Tight clays make additives hard to spread, and fractures channel them, so subsurface investigation and a pilot study should come before full-scale design. It is used mainly for hydrocarbon and chemical spills, with nitrogen and phosphorus key for marine oil spills, and it may also help with herbicides.

soil-env-048.title: Mapping contamination with geographic information systems
soil-env-048.text: At Idrija, Slovenia, soil absorbed mercury from a mine worked for over 500 years. A GIS model mapped how that mercury escapes from the soil, and the emissions peaked in July. GIS in environmental contamination means using geographic information system software to map and analyze contaminants in soil, water and air. Drawing on remote sensing, lidar, GeoAI and WebGIS, spatial analysis flags high-risk metal-contaminated sites for remediation. Spatial interpolation, estimating values between sample points, makes cleanup and monitoring more efficient. Urban soils gather heavy elements from transport, industry and natural weathering, and some of the most contaminated soils surround mines.

soil-env-017.title: Germs in runoff, from livestock yards to drinking water
soil-env-017.text: Runoff can carry disease. Pathogens in runoff are disease-causing bacteria and viruses carried in polluted runoff, a danger chiefly when they reach public drinking water. They include Cryptosporidium parvum, Giardia lamblia, Salmonella, norovirus and other viruses, and parasitic worms. Sources include poorly managed livestock, faulty septic systems, pet waste, over-applied sewage sludge and sewer overflows. Testers often look for coliform bacteria in runoff. These are a common indicator of water pollution but do not themselves cause disease.

soil-env-028.title: Anaerobic bioremediation: cleanup without oxygen
soil-env-028.text: Some pollutants are best broken down where there is no oxygen at all. In anaerobic bioremediation, an added electron donor drives the reduction of oxidized pollutants such as chlorinated solvents, explosives and nitrate. Added organic substrates are first fermented to hydrogen and volatile fatty acids such as acetate and lactate, which feed the bacteria. They go in through wells, by direct push, or in trenches such as biowalls. Slow-release edible oils stay in place longer. The chemistry can stall. Breakdown of the solvent TCE may stop at DCE and vinyl chloride, suspected or known carcinogens, but Dehalococcoides bacteria can carry it on to harmless ethene.

soil-env-027.title: Biopiles and windrows: composting contaminated soil
soil-env-027.text: Contaminated soil can be dug up and treated much like compost. In biopiles and windrows, excavated soil is heaped and aerated to speed microbial breakdown of pollutants. Biopiles use pumps, pushing air in under pressure or drawing it out by suction, to boost aerobic breakdown of petroleum. Windrows are turned regularly, which aerates the soil and spreads contaminants evenly. Both are ex situ methods. These usually cost more than in situ ones, because the soil must be excavated and hauled to a treatment facility.

soil-env-025.title: Biosparging: bubbling oxygen below the water table
soil-env-025.text: Oxygen can be pushed into the saturated ground below the {{ref:soil-water-247}}. Biosparging does exactly that, injecting oxygen, and possibly nutrients, into contaminated saturated zones so that native bacteria degrade pollutants faster. It is the counterpart of {{ref:soil-env-024}}, which aerates the unsaturated zone above. The air must go in hard. In air sparging, it is injected below the water table at a pressure high enough to overcome the water's hydrostatic pressure and the soil's resistance to air flow.

soil-env-024.title: Bioventing: helping soil microbes breathe
soil-env-024.text: Microbes readily break down gasoline, kerosene, diesel and jet fuel when oxygen is plentiful. Bioventing supplies that oxygen, raising the flow of air into the unsaturated zone to speed the natural in situ breakdown of hydrocarbons. It is the commonest aerobic bioremediation. Oxygen serves as the electron acceptor that oxidizes petroleum, PAHs, phenols and other reduced pollutants. Heavier molecules resist biodegradation more. The method is inexpensive, but cleaning a site can take a few years. Below the water table oxygen is scarcer, because water in equilibrium with air holds only 8 to 10 mg/L. There it comes from aerated water, pure oxygen, peroxides or air sparging.

soil-env-031.title: Engineering microbes to clean up pollution
soil-env-031.text: Pseudomonas strains given the lux gene can detect the pollutant naphthalene. Genetically engineered bioremediation uses genetic engineering to design organisms for cleanup, and it is still at the stage of preliminary research. Inserted genes either code proteins that break pollutants down or, like lux, report on pollution. Modified organisms have been made to treat oil spills and break down plastics such as PET. Release raises fears that the genes will pass to other organisms. So engineered organisms can be built to survive only under set conditions, and tagged with bioluminescence genes for tracking.

soil-env-030.title: Why bioremediation is so rarely used
soil-env-030.text: For all its appeal, bioremediation is rarely used. Its drawbacks are slow rates, pollutants that cannot biodegrade, and highly specific microbial needs. Heavy metals and radionuclides do not biodegrade, though they can sometimes be immobilized. Microbes may not fully break a pollutant down, and can leave a more toxic compound behind. Treatment often takes longer than landfilling or incineration, and small test results are hard to scale up to the field. It needs plenty of microbes able to degrade the pollutant in time, preferably native rather than invasive, and control of many environmental factors.

soil-env-029.title: Microbes against pesticide residues
soil-env-029.text: Many sites worldwide are contaminated with agrochemicals, which often resist biodegradation by design. Pesticide bioremediation uses microbes to break down these residues, and it is seen as more promising than other ways of dealing with them. The need is plain. Lindane, a common 20th-century insecticide still produced today, reduces beneficial soil bacteria such as nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria. Grouped strains of Actinobacteria degrade pesticides more efficiently. So far they have been used only in the laboratory, and their cost and scalability are unproven.

soil-env-053.title: Landfarming: tilling oily waste into the topsoil
soil-env-053.text: Ordinary farm equipment can treat refinery waste. In landfarming, contaminated soil, sediment or sludge is mixed into the surface soil and periodically tilled so that microbes degrade the contaminants. It has long handled drill cuttings, oily sludge and other petroleum refinery wastes. A clay or composite liner commonly catches leaching contaminants to protect groundwater. Not everything breaks down. PAHs with more rings, and more chlorinated or nitrated compounds, degrade slowly, and creosote, pentachlorophenol and bunker C oil resist. Inorganic contaminants are not degraded, hydrocarbon levels above 7% poison the microbes, and the microbes turn hydrocarbons into greenhouse gases.

soil-env-201.title: Brownfields: the abandoned sites cities struggle to reuse
soil-env-201.text: The word brownfield was first used in 1992, at a US congressional hearing. Brownfield land is previously developed land, abandoned or underused, that may carry pollution or a risk of it from past industrial use. Abandoned factories, ash ponds, landfills, dry cleaners and gas stations are typical. So are their contaminants: hydrocarbons, solvents, pesticides, asbestos and heavy metals such as lead. Definitions vary between countries, mainly on whether pollution must actually be present. The US EPA counts land whose reuse is complicated by actual or potential contamination. Many sites sit unused for decades because cleanup would cost more than the land is then worth. Unknown buried tanks or drums can raise costs further, so developers often insist on a full site investigation first. Cleanups use heating in place, bioremediation, in situ oxidation, soil vapor extraction, binders that stop leaching, and plants that take up metals. By September 2023 the EPA's brownfields program had readied 134,414 acres for reuse.

soil-env-040.title: Phytodegradation: plants as a green liver
soil-env-040.text: Plants have been called a 'green liver', because they handle foreign compounds much as the human liver does. Phytodegradation, also called phytotransformation, is the use of plants to degrade organic pollutants. It has been proposed for herbicides, trichloroethylene and methyl tert-butyl ether. Researchers have also proposed a pathway by which plants transform the explosive TNT.

soil-env-044.title: Phytoscreening: reading groundwater pollution in tree trunks
soil-env-044.text: A tree can report on the groundwater beneath it. Chlorinated solvents such as trichloroethylene turn up in tree trunks at concentrations related to those in groundwater. Phytoscreening uses plants this way, as biosensors that map contaminant plumes underground. Standard methods take a core from the trunk, often with an increment borer, for laboratory analysis. It could streamline site investigations and lower cleanup costs, but it has not yet been put to practical use.

soil-env-039.title: Phytostabilization: plants that hold pollution in place
soil-env-039.text: Some cleanups never remove the pollutant at all. Phytostabilization uses plants to contain pollutants for the long term by lowering their mobility, holding them near the roots rather than in plant tissue. The plants reduce erosion, runoff and leaching, and make the contaminant less bioavailable. Vegetative caps have been used to stabilize and contain mine tailings. Root mats of meadow grasses may immobilize radioactive materials. The chemistry is fickle, though: some soil amendments reduce mobility at one concentration but increase it at another.
